meta.title: Who really said "Nice guys finish last"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Leo Durocher's 1946 jab at the last-place Giants was "The nice guys are all over there. In seventh place." Sportswriters compressed it into the proverb.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nice guys finish last'?
meta.ogDescription: Durocher's real 1946 line was about the Giants in seventh place. The famous four words are a headline-desk condensation he only later embraced.

answer.label: Not his exact words — a sportswriters’ condensation
answer.authorDates: 1905–1991 · MLB manager whose 1946 dugout jab got compressed into a proverb
answer.sourceLine: The sentiment is genuinely Durocher’s, but the four words are not what he said. On 6 July 1946, needling the last-place New York Giants (and their well-liked manager Mel Ott), he was recorded by sportswriter Frank Graham as saying “The nice guys are all over there. In seventh place.” Headline and digest editors compressed ‘seventh place’ into ‘last place,’ and by the late 1940s Durocher had embraced the bumper-sticker version — eventually using it as the title of his 1975 autobiography.

source.heading: What Durocher actually said

docMeta.dd: Needling the last-place 1946 New York Giants, recorded by sportswriter Frank Graham

source.excerpt: The nice guys are all over there. In seventh place.
trail: Durocher’s actual 1946 words, per Frank Graham’s column, were about the Giants in ‘seventh place,’ not ‘last’ — a Baseball Digest reprint that fall swapped in ‘last place.’
Etymology references treat the four-word proverb as a condensation of the original remark, dated to 1946 and attributed to Durocher.
Baseball historians note that many scholars believe Leo never said the exact four words; even Durocher misquoted himself in his 1975 memoir.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording documented in Frank Graham’s column; seventh place was next-to-last in the 1946 National League. Popular retellings embroider it into a longer dugout speech (“Take a look at them… all nice guys… they’ll finish last”), but the four-word proverb is a later condensation.

sourceLink.text: Barry Popik: the 1946 origin of the phrase

source.rightsNote: The exact four-word phrase has no single authored primary source: it is an anonymous journalistic condensation that evolved across 1946 newspapers and digests. Durocher’s underlying 1946 remark (Frank Graham’s Journal-American column) and his 1975 autobiography of the same title are both post-1931 and would be in copyright, but the proverb itself is a short idiomatic phrase not tied to one copyrightable work.

author.name: Leo Durocher
author.heading: Leo “the Lip” Durocher
author.metaLine: 1905–1991 · Hall of Fame MLB manager & shortstop, "Leo the Lip"
author.bio: Leo Durocher (1905–1991) was one of baseball’s most combustible figures — a scrappy shortstop turned pugnacious manager of the Dodgers, Giants and Cubs, elected to the Hall of Fame in 1994. His running feud with the genial Giants manager Mel Ott produced the 1946 dugout crack that sportswriters polished into “nice guys finish last.” Durocher happily claimed the line for the rest of his life, titling his 1975 memoir after it.

misattribution.heading: What’s misremembered
misattribution.intro: The line is quoted as if Durocher said these exact four words to reporters in 1946. The credit is fairly his, but the wording is not.

items.why: It was minted by headline and digest editors, not spoken verbatim by Durocher; his recorded 1946 line was “The nice guys are all over there. In seventh place.”
Durocher pointed at the Giants in seventh place; a Baseball Digest reprint that fall changed it to ‘last place,’ per the documented condensation.
In his 1975 autobiography he quoted himself incorrectly, 29 years later, in a version his own contemporary record contradicts.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment and the target were genuinely Durocher’s, but the polished four words were compressed by sportswriters and only later adopted by him as his own.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The phrase became a proverb because it says something the culture wanted a snappy way to say — that decency is a competitive liability. It helped that the source was baseball’s most quotable villain, and that the target, Mel Ott, was famously one of the game’s genuinely nice men whose Giants really were sinking toward the cellar.

Durocher never corrected the record — he leaned in, using the line as a personal credo, a 1948 magazine piece, and finally a book title, which is how a garbled dugout aside hardened into a saying quoted far outside sports.
context.pull: He didn’t say the four words — he adopted them.
